name: Finality
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: When Is Done Actually Done?
lesson.summary: Finality is the guarantee that a confirmed transaction cannot later be reversed or reordered, and different consensus mechanisms offer very different strengths of that guarantee.
lesson.body:
Once a transaction, as defined earlier, gets included in a block, a natural question follows: is it actually safe to treat as settled. The answer depends entirely on the consensus mechanism securing the chain, because not every mechanism gives the same kind of promise. Finality is the general term for how strongly and how quickly a system can guarantee that a confirmed transaction will never be undone.

Proof of work chains like Bitcoin offer what is usually called probabilistic finality. A transaction in the latest block is technically still reversible, since a competing chain could, in theory, catch up and overtake it, an event called a reorganization. But every additional block built on top makes that reorganization more expensive to pull off, since an attacker would need to out produce the honest network's accumulated proof of work. This is why many exchanges and merchants wait for a handful of additional confirmations, commonly six on Bitcoin, before treating a large payment as safe. It is a cautious convention rather than a hard rule enforced by the protocol itself, chosen because the odds of a reversal fall to a level most businesses consider acceptable by that point.

Byzantine fault tolerant systems built on something like Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance tend to offer a stronger promise called deterministic, or absolute, finality. Because a supermajority of a known validator set explicitly commits to a value during a structured voting round, as described in the Practical BFT chapter, once that commit threshold is reached there is no lingering possibility of a longer competing history quietly overtaking it later. The transaction is settled the moment enough validators have signed off, full stop, rather than becoming merely less and less likely to be reversed over time.

A simple analogy separates the two. Probabilistic finality is like a promise that gets more trustworthy the longer it survives unchallenged, similar to how a rumor that has held up under a week of scrutiny is more believable than one from an hour ago, but is technically still not proven beyond all doubt. Deterministic finality is more like a notarized signature: once enough authorized parties have formally signed off in the same session, the matter is closed, not merely increasingly likely to stay closed.

This difference has real consequences for anyone building on top of a blockchain. A payment processor accepting Bitcoin has to decide how many confirmations are worth waiting for given the value of the transaction, balancing customer patience against reversal risk. A system relying on a deterministic finality chain can typically treat a committed transaction as done almost immediately after commitment, in practice usually taking a few minutes rather than the roughly hour that cautious Bitcoin users budget for six confirmations. Neither approach is simply better in every situation. They are different tradeoffs between speed, the assumptions a network is willing to make about who is participating, and how much risk a user is willing to accept.
